- **BH procedure:** The procedure is defined as finding the largest rank i where the ordered p-value is at most i·q/m, then rejecting hypotheses with p-values up to that threshold (Let R be the largest i such that q(i) ≤ iq/m ... Then reject H0j if and only if qj ≤ Rq/m.).

steps.text:
I confirmed all three values from the text of the paper itself. One correction to your citation: the example is in **Section 3.2**, "Example of False Discovery Rate Controlling Procedure", on pp. 294–295, not Section 4.

**Source.** I read it on 2026-10-17 from https://errorstatistics.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/benjamini-and-hochberg-searchable-fdr.pdf. This is a scan of the original JRSS-B 57(1) article with an OCR text layer, so it is the paper itself, but transcribed by OCR. The page headers ("294 BENJAMINI AND HOCHBERG [No. 1", "1995] CONTROLLING FALSE DISCOVERY RATE 295") match the published pages. Copy-edit marks in the scanned text ("hy-potheses", "sequen-tially") show the source page itself was scanned. The URL is a mirror on Deborah Mayo's blog site, not the publisher.

**1. The 15 ordered p-values, verbatim:**
> "The ordered P(i)s for the 15 comparisons made are 0.0001, 0.0004, 0.0019, 0.0095, 0.0201, 0.0278, 0.0298, 0.0344, 0.0459, 0.3240, 0.4262, 0.5719, 0.6528, 0.7590, 1.000."

The last value is printed with three decimals ("1.000"), unlike the others.

**2. The level.** You were right: q* = 0.05.
> "Using the FDR controlling procedure with q* = 0.05, we now compare sequentially each P(i) with 0.05i/15, starting with P(15)."

The family-wise error rate (FWER) for Bonferroni is also controlled at 0.05.

**3. Rejection counts, verbatim:**
- **Bonferroni rejects 3:** "Controlling the FWER at 0.05, the Bonferroni approach, using 0.05/15 = 0.0033, rejects the three hypotheses corresponding to the smallest p-values." The paper adds that these are reduced allergic reaction and two aspects of bleeding, not mortality.
- **Hochberg (1988) also rejects 3:** "Using Hochberg's procedure leaves us with the same three hypotheses rejected."
- **BH rejects 4:** "Thus we reject the four hypotheses having p-values which are less than or equal to 0.013." The OCR garbles the sentence just before this ("The first p-value to satisfy the constraint is P<4> as 4 P<4> = = 0.013"). It presumably reads P(4) = 0.0095 ≤ (4/15)·0.05 = 0.013 in print, but I couldn't confirm that sentence's exact symbols. The rest of the passage came through cleanly.

**My own recomputation agrees on all three.** P(4) = 0.0095 is at or below 0.0133, and P(5) through P(9) are each above their thresholds (for example, 0.0201 > 0.0167). The Bonferroni cutoff 0.05/15 = 0.00333 is cleared only by the first three values. Hochberg's procedure also gives 3.

**Secondary source, which agrees:** https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.false_discovery_control.html (read 2026-10-17). The SciPy docs for `scipy.stats.false_discovery_control` reproduce the same 15 values and the 0.05 level. They say Bonferroni rejects "the first three p-values" and that "the first four adjusted p-values fall below 0.05". They cite Neuhaus et al. (1992), JACC 19(5):885–891, and present the example as coming from the BH paper. I found no discrepancies in any value or count.

**Sources I couldn't use:**
- http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~ybenja/MyPapers/benjamini_hochberg1995.pdf is image-only, and I couldn't render it without writing files.
- A Stanford Stats 200 Lecture 11 PDF and a Universitat de València slide deck were unreadable through the fetch tool.
- https://math.mit.edu/~rmd/465/multhyp.pdf returned a 404 error.

**Terminology note.** In the paper's own wording, both Hochberg's procedure and BH are "step-down" procedures, meaning they start at the largest p-value. Modern literature calls BH "step-up" for the same logic. This changes no numbers but could confuse anyone quoting the text.

I didn't write any files. The fetch tool saved the PDFs automatically, and I extracted the text from them in memory.
